haiku-low.q2: It makes one attempt, then three retries 2 seconds apart, then exits non-zero and never becomes ready. Old pods keep serving, so live traffic is unaffected.
haiku-low.q3: A background thread re-reads each key every 5 minutes and swaps in a new non-empty version. If the read fails, it keeps the last good value and logs a warning.
haiku-low.q4: Only in process memory, in a lock-guarded dictionary. Never on disk, in environment variables, or in logs, including the Authorization header.
haiku-low.q5: Prod pods running as orders-api-prod have read-only access. Only the security on-call role can write prod secrets. Engineers are explicitly denied prod reads.
haiku-low.q6: The old keys sit in git history for two years and are treated as leaked, and history is not rewritten. They are harmless only once revoked at the providers after every pod is confirmed on new keys.
haiku-low.q7: Each outbound call runs secrets.get(name) at request time and builds the Authorization header from the current in-memory value, without storing it on the client.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded first. secrets.start() loads all three keys at process start, and /healthz returns 503 until that first load of all three succeeds. Then it returns 200 and the instance is ready. This holds even if the HTTP server is already listening.
sonnet.q2: It makes 1 initial attempt, then retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart. After that it logs the secret name and error class (never a value) and exits non-zero. The pod crashes and never becomes ready. The rollout halts and the old pods keep serving, so live traffic is unaffected.
sonnet.q3: A background daemon thread wakes every 5 minutes, starting 5 minutes after the first load. It re-reads each name separately. If the version id differs and the value is non-empty, it swaps in the new value and version id together under a lock and logs 'secret loaded'. If a read fails, it keeps the last good value, logs a warning with the name and error class, and tries again at the next tick. The failure does not change /healthz. An alert fires if a name has had no successful re-read for more than 15 minutes.
sonnet.q4: Values are held in a process-memory dictionary (value and version id per name) guarded by a lock. They must never appear on disk, in environment variables, or in logs. That also means no Authorization header and no request objects with headers in logs. Version ids may be logged.
sonnet.q5: Read: the orders-api-prod service identity has read-only access to orders-api/prod/*. Engineers are explicitly denied read and write on prod. Write: only the security on-call role. The document does not name any other human who can read prod values.
sonnet.q6: The old keys remain in git history (two years) and in previously built images, and history is not being rewritten. So the old keys are treated as leaked and every key is rotated. The old keys are harmless because they are revoked at the provider at the end, after confirming every pod is on the new keys.
sonnet.q7: The clients no longer copy the key at construction. For each outbound call, the client runs secrets.get('<name>') at the moment of the request, which takes the lock briefly and returns a plain string. It builds the Authorization header from that result and does not store the value on self.
sonnet.q8: This is step 8, done once the rollout is complete and at least 5 minutes have passed. The security on-call or release engineer checks that the cluster lists exactly the expected 4 pods, all on the post-migration image. For each pod and name, the latest 'secret loaded name=... version=...' log line must equal the store's current version id. There must be no refresh-failure warning after that line. A missing or mismatched line means the pod is not confirmed, and that blocks revocation. The evidence is recorded on the ticket.
sonnet.q9: First, check that each provider supports two active keys. Second, set up the store layout and access rules. Third, create new keys at the providers and load them into the store, leaving the old keys active. Fourth, implement the app change that reads from the store, together with removing the keys from the YAML and adding the CI guard in the same PR. Fifth, deploy by rolling update. Sixth, confirm every instance is on the new keys. Seventh, mark old images non-deployable and revoke the old keys at the providers. The code can be built in parallel with steps 2-3, once the dev path has keys.
sonnet.q10: make run starts with APP_ENV=dev and reads orders-api/dev/* from the store. It uses the engineer's own store login and the same code path as production. Those are provider sandbox or test keys. Alternatively, make run-offline uses local stub servers and needs no store access and no keys.
sonnet.q11: Any failure to read any of the three counts, including a missing secret. So it retries as for any failure: 1 initial attempt plus 3 retries, 2 seconds apart. Then it logs the secret name and error class and exits non-zero, and never becomes ready. The document does not describe running with only two keys.
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED. Security has not decided, and the plan sets no schedule or cadence. It is an open question. Rotation is possible without downtime through the step 16 runbook and the 5-minute refresh.
